utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we deal with the evidence of the next witness, there's one thing we would like to clarify with Mr. Hannis. We've all throughout worked with photocopies of P1468, the notes of the Joint Command meetings. There is reference in other documents before the Trial Chamber to a bound book with a ring binder or spiral binder. Do you have that book, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't. I've been trying to track that down since -- well, over the weekend to determine what the situation is. I know in the -- what we call the MIF sheet, it used to be called -- I can't remember, the IF. It's the identification or information sheet that's filled out when evidence is brought into the Tribunal, and it was described as, I think, a blue notebook with a red binder, and I don't know whether we actually received that or if that's how it was described in the inventory that came with it when it when it was presented. As I understand, Madam Del Ponte, who was the Prosecutor, received it from Mr. Djindjic. Now, I know with practically all the original documents that I'm aware of that we get from Serbia, we don't actually get them. We're allowed to look at them and make copies of them. I don't know if that's what happened in this situation or not. I know that when Mr. Djakovic was interviewed by Phil Coo in 2004, he was shown the -- the hard -- hard copy of the exhibit we have been working with, which has the ERN K02284- -- 8412 to 8563, because in his statement at paragraph 34 he says: "I have been shown by Philip Coo a copy of an A4 document entitled Meetings Of the Joint Command For Kosovo And Metohija." And there's a reference to the ERN number. He says, "I recognise this as a copy of my notebook. This is absolutely my hand writing. I could not be a hundred per cent certain whether anyone took any pages from this. Having looked at it, I see that there's some question marks beside some entires to mark where I missed a point or could not fully understand."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, Mr. Hannis, but what actually happens to the originals of evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The original evidence we have I understand are kept in our evidence vault, and when we check in our evidence vault to see what is there for what's our exhibit P1468, what we have is a Xerox copy. Now, I've tried to contact Phil Coo over the weekend because he's my most immediate link in the chain back to see if he can provide us any additional information, but I haven't been able to actually speak with him. He may be in later this morning. He's working at another Tribunal now, Your Honour, not in this country, and that's -- that's where it stands at the moment. I don't have any further information, but I'm trying to find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. THE PROSECUTOR: And we do have a hard copy of what was in the vault if you want it for the witness. I don't know if it's better than what's in e-court. It's a printout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next witness, then, will be Chamber witness Milan Djakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Djakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: First of all, may I thank you for responding to the Chamber's invitation to give evidence here. It will come as no surprise to you that your name has been mentioned on occasions in the course of our evidence in a number of contexts, and the Chamber considered it would be helpful to our consideration of the case to have a further explanation from you of certain matters. There are formalities at the beginning of the evidence that I'll deal with first of all. Is your full name Milan Djakovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're a retired general of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did you retire?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The 31st of December, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And which specific rank did you hold?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is your final position? Which post did you retire from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I retired from the post of deputy commander of the 1st Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The 23rd of October, 1948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Since retiring from the army, have you had other employment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This case concerns principally 1998 and 1999. Can you give us an account of the posts in the army that you held during 1998 and 1999, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998, I was chief of the department for operations and teaching in the command of the Pristina Corps from the 25th of December, 1997, up until -- up until around the 20th of January, 1999. After that, I took up the position of the chief of department for operations and training in the command of the 3rd Army, and I stayed on until the end of the war, carrying out those duties, that is. On the 4th of October, 1999, I was sent to the national defence school or college in Belgrade where I stayed on until 1999 -- or, rather, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's sufficient for my purposes at the moment. When you were with the Pristina Corps, who was the commander of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Pristina Corps was General Bojovic. When I came for the first time, that is to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I should have made it clear. In 1998 when you were with the Pristina Corps, who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998, it was General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And when you joined the 3rd Army, who was the commander of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Also General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you recollect when he moved from the Pristina Corps to the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly before I was transferred to the command of the 3rd Army. That is sometime in February. I think it was February, or was it the end of January, or February 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In both the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army, did you work closely with him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you look now, please, at P1468, which will appear on the screen, but Mr. Hannis has volunteered to give you a hard copy of the document. You actually may have your own copy there. Do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, but -- but I got one here when I came to The Hague two days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you have it with you in court, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have it here with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will be helpful if you use that document rather than what's on the screen. It's a copy of something else, as you can see. What is it a copy of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a copy of a notebook that I kept when I went to attend meetings with the MUP organs, that is to say the organs of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you -- if you go to -- I'll need to give you a page reference, which may be difficult in -- it will be impossible in the Serbian version, which you have. If you could go to the entry for the 21st of October, 1999 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At that point -- from that point onwards, were you responsible for the notebook?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in a way I was responsible because it's my notebook, and I gave it to the assistant due to the engagements I had on account of the assignments given to me by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who was that assistant?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: That assistant was Colonel Ratko Tesevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what post did he hold at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: He was the assistant chief of the department for operations and teaching in the department for operations and teaching. That is to say that he was my number-one assistant, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there a change in your own responsibilities at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was that change?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the change had to do with the arrival of the OSCE mission, because I as the chief of department was primarily in charge of plans, and I was assigned a task by General Pavkovic to prepare a new variant for the arrival of the OSCE mission in relation to the withdrawal of forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who took over your post as head of operations and training, or did you retain that post?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I retained that post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I've seen somewhere a reference to responsibilities being handed to General Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in 2004 that I spoke and made an uncertain claim, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's my responsibility for your microphone going off. It was an accident. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, I did not over -- I did not hand over the notebook to General Stefanovic, and that was a doubt that I expressed in 2004 because General Stefanovic came considerably later to assume this duty, that is to say, sometime in December, between the 15th and 20th of December, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting from the 21st of October onwards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: That is the handwriting of Colonel Tesevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: After the 21st of October, did you continue to have access to this book?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I tried to remember after this conversation all the details that were involved, so as far as I can remember on the 24th of October, an order came from the army command in connection with setting up archives in relation to all the documents related to combat operations in 1998. As I was completing my duties in terms of plans related to taking in the OSCE mission, I talked to Colonel Tesevic, and when I assigned a task to him in relation to archiving documents, I gave him an order to put that notebook in the archives, as well, together with the other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you see it again after that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: That notebook?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The original. I never saw it again from that moment when he brought it to my office and when I gave it back to him practically the same instant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know how it came to -- at least its contents came to arrive in the hands of the Office of the Prosecutor here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not have the notebook, and I did not have the possibility to get ahold of that notebook, and I didn't really have any special need to do so or did anyone ask me to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's been suggested that there are changes to the handwriting in the book even during the period when -- when you had it. It may or may not be a matter of any importance, but could you look at the entry for the 25th of July, 1998. Sorry, it's my mistake. The following day, the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've got the 26th of July. You'll see there that the first person who is recorded as speaking is General Pavkovic. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Then he's followed by another person. What was the name of the other person?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, halfway through there is a -- just give me a second until I see the English. Yes. Sorry. There's a reference. I think it's to Weaknesses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, under that, from that point on, is that also your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, as you look at the page, you can understand why someone might think the top half is written by -- the part for -- the first part for Pavkovic down to Weaknesses is written by one person, and the following part including what's attributed to General Lukic is written by someone else.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I see that, but I'm sure, 100 per cent sure, that it's not someone else. I know my own handwriting very well, and there's no chance. I mean, there were these two variants that I wrote, but I don't know. Perhaps there was an interruption in the meeting or something. It is my handwriting, for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can we go back to -- just while we're at this point in the notes, can we go back to the 25th of July, and that's one-page back.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me a moment until the English appears on the screen. Thank you. Yeah, further up, please, so that we can see the entry attributed to Gajo. There's a reference to a person called Gajo. What's his proper name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: His full name is David Gajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the position he held?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, his position was in the state security sector. He was one of the assistant heads. I don't know whether he was directly Mr. Stanisic's assistant, but I know that he was an assistant in the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you read for us, please, what is said or -- what's said under his name there. Just read it aloud. Read aloud what you've written.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. "Terror continues with the activities related to the bringing in of weapons through Gora and Has. New KLA staffs are being set up."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help you there. What is Gora and Has?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Gora and Has are areas close to the Republic of Albania. Gora is in the Dragas municipality, and Has is an area south-west of Djakovica in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and it extends into the Republic of Albania. This whole area is called Has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue to read, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: "Preparations are carried out in the villages in Baranski Lug. "In Malisevo, the supplies of food and fuel are scant. "In Djakovica, the situation is getting more complex in the villages at the outskirts. "The president of the DSK in Pec asked for a more realistic demand to be put in. "In the village of Ljeskovac, Prizren municipality, four groups have been set up to attack the settlement of Tusus and Prizren. "Terrorists from Suva Reka are linking up with the terrorists from Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what do you mean by the --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- the DSK in Pec?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the abbreviation for the Democratic Union of Kosovo. It is their political organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that this is your -- these are your notes in your notebook. What were you noting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I took notes. The first time that I attended one of those meetings, I didn't have an idea of what notes I would be taking, but as the meetings progressed I noted down things that I thought would provide me with some information and data that would assist me in the performance of my duty at my post since in the command I was in charge of implementing the coordination with the -- with various entities in the field. That was my function, my post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Two matters immediately arise from that. What were the various entities in the field that you were responsible for implementing coordination with?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was responsible for all the entities that were in any way working together with the Pristina Corps in the Kosovo territory, including the entities and other structures outside of the territory of Kosovo, but that was done only with the approval of the corps commander and the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you list the most important ones, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, the ministry -- the organs of the Ministry of the Interior, primarily the staff in Pristina; then with the administration of the Ministry of Defence in Pristina, which was located in the same building where the corps command was; then with the units of the 3rd Army that were relocated to other areas in Kosovo that were either stationed there or had been brought in; and with the units and organs of the air force and air defence and the communications units to the extent that I was able to do so, and that involved, also, other organs from the corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other matter that immediately arises is, how did you come to attend your first meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, with the organs of the Ministry of the Interior, we started having meetings as early as in April and May 1998, meetings that were -- that involved the army and the Ministry of the Interior organs. I attended a couple of such meetings before this meeting on the 22nd. On the 22nd, General Pavkovic called me around 11.00 or 12.00. It was in the morning, anyway, and the day before he had come back from Belgrade, so on the 21st he came back from Belgrade, and on the 22nd he invited me to his office, and he told me this: Djakovic, you might as well accompany me to this meeting in the MUP. I asked him, what am I supposed to do? And he said, I don't want to be there alone; you should take a notebook and just jot down everything you think you might need. I left his office, and I waited for the general summons. I waited for him to call me to go with him to this meeting in MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So he invited you to go, and you went with him. Now --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was it that you recorded in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: At the first meeting. Are you talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At the meetings in general. I want you to tell me what -- not the specific things that you wrote down but the general nature of what you recorded at the various meetings that you attended thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. As those meetings progressed, after three or four meetings, I already got a kind of a picture as to what I should jot down, what I should record, and what would be of interest to me. So at the first meeting, I started noting -- so we're talking about the 22nd. The meeting was opened by Mr. Minic, so that's when I started making those notes. I didn't write the part that was above that, if we're talking about the 22nd. From where it says "Memorandum" to item 8 where you see my name, I jotted that down on our return to the command or the next day. I can't remember now. It may have been the next day when I actually wrote that down, and I wrote first of what Mr. Gajic said, his report, and then everything that is written here. At the meetings that followed, I mostly recorded the questions or issues that related to the security, brief reports by Generals Pavkovic and Lukic regarding the situation in the units of the Pristina Corps and the units of the Ministry of the Interior, and comments made by other participants in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you record what was said at these meetings accurately?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that they spoke quite fast, so I can't be 100 per cent sure that I recorded everything verbatim. In particular, the civilians, the political representatives of the Republic of Serbia and of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, because their terminology was unfamiliar to me as a soldier, the political terminology. So I tended to translate it into military-speak. So I may have done that as I made those notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How selective were you in what you recorded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was rather selective except when it came to the data that was obtained from the state security. I tried to get as much information as I could because this information was very important to me. And another thing, I had to put this information in order and to give it to the security commander, Colonel Stojanovic, who is now the general, and he was the chief of the security in the Pristina Corps. And General Pavkovic also had to inform the army commander about the key information provided at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before these meetings began to take place, did the army have difficulty getting information from the state security?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, to a considerable extent, and I remember I have to establish a connection with a document that was brought in regarding the exchange of communication a long time before this meeting, a long time before the political representatives from Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia came. That's the operational report. As far as I can recall, the first one was drafted on the 10th of July, as far as I can recall. I did not see this first document, but I think that the date is the 10th of July. If you would allow me, I would like to explain how this came about. I explained to General Pavkovic that I had problems in making assessments of the Siptar terrorist forces and that Colonel Stojanovic had the same problems. He was responsible together with the chief of the intelligence service with formulating the first item in the report, and I asked him if through Lukic and Gajic he could make sure that information flowed in that would make it possible for me and Stojanovic to put together this first item in the order for the use of forces, and he said he would try. And after a few days, I received the first report from the Ministry of the Interior and from Mr. Gajic, and this practice continued up until the end of the year or thereabouts. Since I received -- after I received the report from them, I drafted an internal document, and then as a favour to them I provided information to them about the status of the army and the disposition of the army units so that they could coordinate those activities when they were drafting their plans, and this practice, again, continued up until the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: After Colonel Tesevic takes over, the name "Gajo" -- let me start again. After he takes over, instead of the name "Gajo" there appears the name "Goja" from time to time. Is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand. What was the other name that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Goja, G-o-j-a.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know that name. It's probably the same person, but Mr. Radovic accompanied -- Miro Radovic accompanied Mr. Gajic or Gajo, so his name could be mentioned in places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did you do with the record that you made at each meeting after the meeting was over?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after the meeting was over, I had a look at the notebook to see whether there was anything of interest to me, and then I would give the information to the security organs. I would give them the information about what Gajovic and Radovic had said, so -- to the intelligence service -- to the security organs so that they use it for their activities. Colonel Djindjic [Realtime transcript read in error "Djinovic"] also used it for quite a long time. He was the assistant chief of security in the 3rd Army. He worked with Colonel Stojanovic. I gave the notebook to him, too, and he jotted down some things from the notebook, but it was in the office. I didn't allow -- allow anyone else to use the notebook. Those who wanted to use the notebook that I allowed them to use it, they could do it in my office, or I would simply relay the information to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you distribute copies of the notebook or pages from the notebook to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Up until the moment the notebook was put in the archive, I never allowed anyone to make any copies of the notebook. Now, somebody may have done that without my knowledge; I can't tell that, but I personally never allowed that to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 17, line 5 is Djindjic, not Djinovic. Colonel Djindjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Djindjic, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you could turn now to the outside cover of the document you have there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you write the title there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The title is computer-written at the Centre for Automatic Data-Processing. I assume that it was Colonel Tesevic who asked somebody to type this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you then go to the first meeting, the 22nd of July, that's just over one page, can you read what it says at the top of that page?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: "Meeting of the Joint Command for KiM."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So right from the outset, you were referring to this as the Joint Command for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that your idea?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult now to give you an answer in just a few words whether it was my idea or not, but that was not an idea that cropped up at this meeting. It's an idea that dated from a period before that. We called it the meetings of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija a long time before the political organs arrived in Kosovo, and there are some documents to corroborate that. I remember there's a document from the 6th of July, 1998. That was the first time that we really wrote down on paper the meeting of the Joint Command. That was the first time that the Joint Command was mentioned, and I myself put it down here because I had left half of the page blank, and the next day, together with General Pavkovic -- actually, I spoke to General Pavkovic, and I asked him, what should I do about those meetings; how should I make records of them. And he said, in the same way that you had -- have until now. And that's how it remained. And after the second meeting, the meetings were styled the sessions of the Joint Command because the gentleman from the republic and from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia referred to those meetings as sessions, and up until the very end this is how they were styled, sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sessions is -- is a formal term for a meeting, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the problems for the Trial Chamber is that there's a lot of formality in the name Session and Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, and it's easy to -- to jump to the conclusion without reading the content and hearing the evidence that this must have been a body which directed activities. Was it such a body?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that this was a body that directed anything in particular because I know how the chain of command functioned in the army, and I have some knowledge about how it functioned in the Ministry of the Interior, so no decisions were made here. And I really went through all those records in detail, and there are no decisions, no orders of any organs except for what General Lukic or General Pavkovic are saying related to the decisions that they or their superior officers made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you left each meeting, did you know what decisions would be taken in the formal command structure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No decisions were made here. Decisions had already been made at General Samardzic's, and I don't know whether it was General Lukic who made the decisions in the MUP or whether he received decisions from the minister of the interior in Belgrade, but the decisions were made on the basis of the army commander and the plans that we submitted to the army commander for his approval. No decisions were made here about the use of the forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What would you say was the principal purpose of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I've thought a long time about this, and I think that the main purpose was the exchange of information. That's number one because based on my analysis, about 35 to 60 per cent of all the meetings deal with the security situation. The rest of the meeting was devoted to brief -- briefings by General Pavkovic and General Lukic about what the army personnel and the MUP personnel had done in the course of that day, and the rest was devoted to the comments made by other participants. Mr. Sainovic, I have to say, took the floor on most occasions to talk about foreign policy issues. Mr. Minic dealt with issues related to the functioning of the local authorities, municipality/district level, and Mr. Andjelkovic spoke about civilians protection issues. Mr. Matkovic spoke about the economy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In light of that explanation, it is very difficult for someone who is not a military person, like myself, to understand the use of the term "command" to describe this body. Can you help me to understand why it was called a Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can. The first document that we wrote where we refer to a Joint Command is dated the 6th of July, 1998. That is an order issued by General Pavkovic on the basis of an order issued by the army commander on the prohibition of the use of units without approval of the army commander. Let me also mention that he did know of this term "the Joint Command," and he attended some meetings of the Joint Command. When I was first given the task after the meeting with members of the MUP to regulate the question of relations between the MUP and the army, quite simply it wasn't clear to me what it was that I was supposed to put there because these were documents in a text, and when the general said, "Put 'Joint Command,'" I then asked whether the documents would be sent to the Ministry of the Interior, and he said, no; this only has to do with us so that our organs know that these questions have been agreed upon with members of the MUP. So the first document is dated the 6th of July, 1998, considerably before the representatives of the republican and federal organs came to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but it's the -- it's the expression "command." What was it commanding?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: "Command" pertained to the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps. That is to say that when we talked about the variant as to what we should put in the text, I suggested to him another variant: Staff of the MUP and the command of the Pristina Corps, and the general said, that's long; how can we put all that down? So then through an exchange of comments, we came to the conclusion, the two of us, that it would be best to put "Joint Command" because that denoted the command of the MUP staff and the command of the Pristina Corps, no one else. General Lukic and General Pavkovic, no one else. And the commander of the army was aware of that, too, and that is what he used as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How frequently did it meet? In other words, is that record complete, or are there pages missing from it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is hard for me to know now whether there is a particular page missing, but I do have some observations to make. On the 24th of August, if you can -- no. No. The 24th -- just a moment, please. The 24th of August. I think -- I think that this was not completed. I have an explanation that is possible in terms of why I did not do this up until the end, and that is that I think that General Simic asked for me on that evening, around 8.00 in the evening, as soon as the meeting started. Through the duty officer in the operations centre, he asked me to explain to him some questions related to the use of ammunition. I informed General Pavkovic about that, and he said, go ahead and see what that is all about, and I went out. I went to the operations centre, and I spoke on the telephone to General Simic in relation to the ammunition spent, and I spent quite a bit of time there because we had to deal with some professional issues fully, and at the end we concluded what the best way of reporting on the use of ammunition would be because there were some controversial issues in that regard. There was another meeting that I noticed that is another interruption. So I assume that two or three times while these meetings were held when I was there, I went out because the duty officers asked me to come. Some did not manage to resolve problems that cropped up on their own, so they would call me as chief of the department, and one or two times perhaps I was - how to put this - late or I did not attend all meetings fully. So five or six times in total, perhaps, there were meetings where I did not fully participate or where I simply did not attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where did the meetings normally take place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, usually they were held at the building of the provisional Executive Council. That was in the centre of Pristina about 200 or 250 metres away from the corps command and the MUP Staff Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did they ever take place anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: These meetings of this kind were held -- well, the first meeting was held at the ministry building, as far as I can remember, the building of the Ministry of Interior, meetings of this kind, whereas the coordination meetings between the MUP organs and myself as the chief who was responsible for further coordination were held at the building of the corps command and at the MUP building. So most often, this was Colonel Adamovic, one of colonel Lukic's assistant commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To what extent was the Grand Hotel in Pristina used for the purposes of the army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Grand Hotel is right next door to the military building, to the military hotel, and the command of the Pristina Corps. It was used at one point in time. That was on the 29th. I remember that very well, when the MUP building was bombed, the building of the Ministry of the Interior. That is -- well, it happened during the night, and we were sleeping at the hotel, the military hotel, Sloboda. And during the night, there was an explosion. We ran out onto the terrace, and we saw the MUP building on fire. We sounded an alert at the command very quickly, and we went out to the underground premises of the military hotel and of the military centre and the underground rooms that are right next door to the Grand Hotel. These are some trading companies or something like that. I don't know. These are some halls. These are rooms that are not really properly appointed. I mean, there were some tables, chairs there, things that they didn't need and that they just left down there. If you allow me to say this, we stayed there -- or, rather, I stayed there perhaps for another seven or eight days with a group of officers. The corps command left after a day or two, once the question of organising signals and communication was regulating and also the messenger service, the courier service in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there also a basement in the Grand Hotel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: There were some rooms where there were some tables, chairs, some kind of furniture, boxes, whatever else was there. These are enormous halls down there, underneath the hotel, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So a similar arrangement exists in both the military hotel and the Grand Hotel. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did the army use the basement of the Grand Hotel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that we used part of the staff, the assistant staff, that is to say, the messenger service. That is where mail was exchanged because we could not regulate the arrival of couriers straight away to the command post. That is where we had an exchange of mail, and I stayed there with three or four officers who were in charge of the direct security for the military command, the military hotel, and the army centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry I've repeated the question, but it was to do with the way in which your answer was translated into English. It's now -- it's now clear. What about upper floors of the Grand Hotel? The first floor, was it used for the purposes of the army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, never. There were ordinary soldiers there and this group of officers, including myself, regulating these questions such as the security of the building. Everything in the building of our command was still there, in the basement of that building of ours, and the communications centre remained there, and we could not relocate that, and we were afraid that somebody might break into these military buildings, and 40 or 50 soldiers stayed there, and a few officers, until all of this was all sort of put in order, the general situation in this territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was your understanding of the role of Mr. Lukic, General Lukic, of the MUP in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can just give my opinion on the basis of these few contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Your understanding, your impression of what role he held.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that General Lukic had powers to command units of the Ministry of the Interior, primarily the PJPs. Now, what role he had in relation to the Secretariats of the Interior, I don't know, because I know that the minister had a direct link with the secretariats of the interior. At least, that is what I heard from the members of the MUP. Now, whether General Lukic -- well, I suppose he did because in particular I had this conversation with him when he told me that he was sending dispatches to secretariats of the interior; that is to say that he had certain contacts with the secretariats of the interior as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who apart from him from the MUP attended your Joint Command meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, General Djordjevic attended, General Obrad Stevanovic. I think that Mijatovic was there, too, one of the assistants of General Lukic. Well, probably one or two other people as well. Say five or six people came to attend these meetings from the Ministry of the Interior. If one person couldn't come, then somebody would come to replace him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had some evidence in this case that the purpose of the Joint Command was to coordinate the activities of the MUP and the VJ because of difficulties in relation to that caused by the MUP. Is there any substance in that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, partly. I would have to mention the first document that is mentioned in relation to the difficulties involved, but not that it was the MUP that was to be blamed but that the relations between the army and the MUP had not been regulated. This is a document dated the 13th of May. I remember that very well because the document has to do with Security Day, the 13th of May, when Colonel Stojanovic at the request of the army commander together with the operations organ wrote an evaluation of the security situation primarily at the border, and in this evaluation there was information about the strength of forces, their groups, their grouping, and what is mentioned is that cooperation was not organised with the MUP at a required level and the army commander is asked to regulate this. May I proceed? The army commander reacts practically within a few days. He sends the chief of staff and a group of officers to the IKM of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica, the forward command post, and General Simic is involved in the activities of the interdepartmental staff of the MUP in Pec as coordinator. As for General Pavkovic, through an order he authorises him to coordinate activities with the MUP on the entire territory of Kosovo. The first major coordination or better coordination, if I can put it that way, took place when the road between Pec and Decani was deblocked by the order of the interdepartmental staff in Pec and in the area where the MUP in part acted in coordination on deblocking these roads leading to Prizren and Djakovica. Later on, this cooperation went from strength to strength, and I can say here that as the person in charge of this cooperation in the command I did not have any problem of getting information from the MUP, from the state security, and also with providing them with information that was relevant to them and that had to do with the command of the Pristina Corps. And I think that this cooperation got better and better as the situation became increasingly complicated in the territory itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the meetings continue into 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that I handed over my duty between the 20th and 25th of January - I don't recall the exact date - and I stayed for another 10 or 15 days there at the command of the Pristina Corps, and after that I went to Nis to assume my duties there. I did not attend meetings any more with members of the Ministry of the Interior. I can only recall the contacts that I had with them sometime on the 19th of April, 1999, when General Pavkovic issued an order -- or, rather, the order of the Chief of General Staff in terms of resubordinating the MUP. And I saw General Stojanovic from MUP and a few other people, Vlahovic in Pec, when I went there to investigate some situations regarding camps in Istok. Those are the two situations I can recall now. At any rate, I ceased these contacts because I assumed other duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were no longer in the same position, but did meetings of the Joint Command continue into 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, after October there were no such meetings, and I did not hear from any members of the Pristina Corps, the organs that were subordinated to me, that they ever went to meetings of the Joint Command, and they did have meetings with members of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in 1999 there were orders issued under the title "Joint Command." Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can give you my opinion that probably the colonel who replaced me in that position probably -- well, continued writing that as the title, "Joint Command for KiM," in order to have these documents show that coordination between the MUP and the military was carried out. I don't have any other explanation because these are documents that only regulated coordination between the army and the MUP. I did see a few documents because they were shown to me in 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you look now, please, at one of our exhibits, 6D716. It will appear on the screen. Just have a quick look at the page that's on the screen, and then would you -- you'll be shown the last -- the last page of the document. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a cliche, as we say, a cliche in terms of an order. Well, not only of an order. It has to do with information on the deployment of the MUP forces as for what the army had until then and what it had summed up on the basis of information collected over the course of one year. So that was all transformed into a particular form of order as to what this kind of order should look like in tentative terms, but you see here where it says "The operations zone of Lab," "the operations zone as of Salja and Bajgora," all the units were referred to for which we had information that they were operating in that area, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who were you giving an order to or drafting an order for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: This is not an order. This is a form, a form of order as to what the form or format of an order should be for units of the MUP or, rather, MUP detachments. Because after all, we have to admit that the army was more trained from that point of view in terms of writing such documents, so we simply wanted to help, to help the members of the MUP so that they can formulate these documents as -- as they should be formulated, in tentative terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who did you give it to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: This document was not logged, and it was not supposed to be logged. It was supposed to be given to the MUP personnel so that they could use it to produce documents that would more or less correspond to the documents produced by the military, but they didn't have to accept any of the information provided herein because this was just there to help them see how an order should be formulated. Because you can see here this document is not logged. It is just a format for a type of document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You drafted it, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who did you give it to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I gave it to the assistant of General Lukic, Mr. Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have to have a break at this stage, General, for 20 minutes or so. Would you please leave the courtroom with the usher while we have the break, and we will resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is coming in, it's come to my attention that through some good detective work we've located the original of P1468. Apparently, it was submitted in the Milosevic trial and has been in the vault with the Registry. Mr. Hajder has now obtained it and has personal possession of it at the moment. I would ask that the Court direct that it temporarily be released from the Milosevic case for use with this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The document Mr. Hajder has put his hand on is also plainly a photocopy. It's not the handwritten version that we would like to see. It's blue, and if it did have a spiral binder it's missing, and the contents are plainly photocopies. So since these do not at the moment add anything -- well, one thing we could ask the -- the -- just a moment. It might help, I think, even from the point of view of its appearance to ask the witness about the outside cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We may be getting closer to the original version of this, Mr. Djakovic. I'm sure we haven't actually got all the way to it, but could you just have a look at this document, which was an exhibit in the trial of Milosevic, and tell me if the cover bears any resemblance to the cover of the original.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The cover was a hard cover of an A4 size notebook, and there was nothing written of it at the time when I had the notebook in my possession, up until the 14th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just return that now to the court usher. I don't think there's any need for us to give it any official record number in this case, and we'll return it to whence it came. One of your answers towards the end of -- of the last session, Mr. Djakovic, you could perhaps amplify for us. I asked you: In 1999 there were orders issued under the title "Joint Command;" can you explain that, and you gave an explanation. Could you try to explain that to me again, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the only explanation I see is that this was an element of coordination between the army and the MUP and that this was the reason why the Joint Command for KiM was put there. I stressed in the earlier part of my testimony that as for the MUP Staff Command and the Pristina Corps command, I saw these two as the Joint Command because the initial documents preceded by far this command that is allegedly mentioned here, the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. So as far as I'm concerned, the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps command formed the Joint Command because we dealt together with any issues related to coordination or concerted action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take it from that answer and the earlier one that there were orders issued in 1998 under the title "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: There were excerpts from the decision of the commander. So those that we did were excerpts from decisions of the commander, but that's not an order. It does not have command authority. It is an excerpt for the purpose of coordination, and it is a prerequisite for the commander's decision to be actually implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm just trying to identify an example of an order from 1999 so that you can see what I'm talking about. Have a look on the screen at P1878. Now, that's the sort of document I'm talking about. Were there similar documents in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I -- well, as far as 1998 is concerned, I know that well because I did most of the work as did my assistants, but in 1998 there was an order from the Pristina Corps command, and excerpts from the decision of the commander were done as the document meant to assist the coordination with the MUP in order for them to be able to do their own documents. And I can see that it says here "An order from the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija," and the date is the 15th of April. I have had an opportunity to look at this document before, but I didn't quite get your question, the specific question relating to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question is whether a similar format of order was used in 1998 with the heading "Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but as excerpts from the decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Excerpts from which decisions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The decisions of the corps commander or army commander. In other words, the Ministry of the Interior was given elements from the decisions in order for it to be able to coordinate things that were within its purview. So only those excerpts from the order were given to them that related to the Ministry of the Interior, elements that they coordinated too. And it is important to note here that in 1998 I did most of the coordination with General Obrad Stevanovic regarding the PJPs and with Colonel Adamovic, one of the assistants to General Lukic, and with Mijatovic quite seldom, in fact, because he would mostly would refer me to Colonel Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We may be talking at cross-purposes here. Could we see the last page of this, please. There must be another English page. Now, this is a complete order signed by the Joint Command, it would appear. Were there similar orders in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that the Pristina Corps orders were signed by General Pavkovic. As far as I can recall, from this decision by the commander on the basis of previous arrangements with the MUP we would extract the elements that pertained to the MUP and provided them to them so that they could do their own plans. I know documents from 1998 bearing the signature of General Pavkovic, but excerpts were made for the needs of the ministry. I'm not sure now. I would have to look at a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's look at paragraph 4 of this one. That's number -- section number 4. And the next page, please, also. Yes. Just hold on until the witness has a chance to read that. Just read it very quickly, just the format. The detail is not of significance for present purposes. And then can we take the English to the next page, please, so that we can see 5.1, which at the foot of the B/C/S. And --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Should I read it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. We'll now turn over your page so that you see the rest of paragraph 5. Now, who is that order destined for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: As for this action at the Rugova gorge, I am familiar with it because I was in Pristina at the time. Our 58th Brigade was stationed in the Pec area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you just tell me who this document would be sent to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: This document would be sent to the Ministry of the Interior as an element of coordination with the MUP forces that were designated to carry out action in the Rugova gorge because the 58th Brigade was there only to block the roads leading out from the Rugova gorge to Pec. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would it also be sent to the 125th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: If there is anything that pertains to it, then for sure, yes, it would be sent to the 125th if it had any impact on the actual execution of this task. I would have to read the task that was assigned to the 125th to see whether it would be sent to it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, go back one page, and you'll see it at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since -- yes, yes, I can see it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I know that this is a repetition of an earlier question, but it's for -- from the point of view of clarifying the system that's operating, not the details of the particular activity here. In 1998, were similar documents being issued to the MUP and to the army units involved in actions such as this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, similar, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: With the name "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were some documents under the name of "Joint Command." That was the basis for their action within the overall system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who would be responsible for sending out this document to the MUP or giving it to the MUP, the one on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: That would be -- you mean who was personally responsible. Personally responsible would be the chief of the operations organ or somebody -- one of his assistants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the person who succeeded you in the Pristina Corps. Is that the person?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And would that --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would that be the person who was responsible for sending it to the 125th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you know of the existence of a body called the MUP staff for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was Adamovic part of the MUP staff for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I know from conversations that Adamovic was one of the assistants together with Mijatovic, but the Adamovic that I knew from the MUP staff, I think there was another Adamovic, but I don't know where he worked. The Adamovic that I know worked in the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And he is the one that you met in relation to transmitting information to the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did he give you information about the strength and location of MUP forces and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I couldn't have done it without him and without other MUP organs, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you hand him extracts from maps related to actions that the VJ were planning?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998, I provided excerpts from the decisions of the commander as elements that they needed. We worked together, so they took part in drafting those plans - Adamovic, General Obrad Stojanovic - through decisions, which of the units would be used, and once this technical part was over, they got the part that pertained to the MUP, and we took the part that pertained to the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the decisions were in -- made up of two elements. There's the narrative in a document such as the one on the screen, and there is a map, which sets out the project as well. Which of these was it that was passed to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are -- the MUP had both documents because those two documents were inseparable. You couldn't have one without the other, and they were the basis for the MUP to be able -- or, rather, for the detachment commanders to be able to do their own assessments and to make their own decisions in accordance with the actual situation. So the detachment commander, after receiving the excerpts, needed four or five hours at least to work on a document to be able to do his order and to draw in the decision two levels down in accordance with the instruction on keeping the working map. So he couldn't carry out combat action on the basis of this document. This document was, rather, the basis for his drafting documents for two levels down, battalion and brigade [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 38, 5. I believe the witness said battalion and detachment, not brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what we were discussing just now. By "detachment" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assumed that. That's why I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. By "detachment," are you referring to a MUP detachment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would that be a PJP detachment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the PJP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I want to ask you now something about the reporting arrangements between the Pristina Corps, the 3rd Army, and the Supreme Command Staff, and the reason I want to ask you about that is because there were four locations involved. The 3rd Army had both a command and a forward command post, and the Pristina Corps had a command and a forward command post, and we've heard evidence, also, that there was insistence at one time in 1999 that the Pristina Corps had to report not only to the 3rd Army but also directly to the Supreme Command Staff. Now, am I right in thinking that this is particularly within your field of operation, the whole question of the reporting regime between the Pristina Corps and the other elements of the army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely, because the operations centre of the Pristina Corps was under my command -- or perhaps I shouldn't say command, but under my control directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're talking now about 1998. Is that -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Where was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? I didn't understand. Who was where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where was the operations centre of the Pristina Corps? Was it at the Pristina Corps command, or was it at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The operations centre, the main operations centre, was located at the Pristina Corps command, and the -- there was an operations centre established at the forward command centre because for it to be able to function normally it has to have this element, the operations centre, in place. So there where General Lazarevic was at the forward command post, that's where the reporting line was set up going in the direction of the Pristina Corps, and you said yourself that at one point he provided direct reports to the General Staff of the army about the situation at the border. That was for practical reasons, to speed up the relaying of the information, the flow of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To avoid confusion, I'm thinking when I make that comment about the position when he was the commander of the Pristina Corps, which is 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what's at issue here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. When you -- we have to remember that General Lazarevic over the period we're concerned about had more than one post. He was the chief of staff of the Pristina Corps, then the commander of the Pristina Corps. Now, when you -- when we talk about direct reporting to the Supreme Command Staff, I'm talking about during the wartime period. Are you saying that there was also an arrangement in 1998 to report directly to the Supreme Command Staff or to the supreme defence -- the chief of --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Nothing was -- nothing changed because instead of General Lazarevic, Colonel Zivkovic was sent to the forward command post. He was the chief of staff of the Pristina Corps. So simply the reporting system from Djakovica through Pristina, the 3rd Army forward command post at the Kosovski Junaci barracks and later on in Gracanica all the way up to Belgrade functioned in the same manner. There were no changes there. The only thing that changed were the actual persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the Pristina Corps reporting was to the 3rd Army command in Nis; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in -- during the war where was General Pavkovic most of the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: From the moment General Pavkovic assumed his duties, his area of responsibility was extremely large. It extended from the left wing of the army, which was at the Danube River facing Romanian border and down towards Bulgaria, Macedonia, and down to Albania, and there was a border or boundary with the 2nd Army in the Sandzak area. So that was a huge territory, and he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not my question. I'm sorry to interrupt you, but my question was: Where was he located during the war, he personally?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: He was in Nis and in the field and in Pristina. So I can't now tell you specifically where he was at any given moment, but once he assumed his duties he spent more time in Nis, but then he went back to Pristina after a while. So it was a large area, and he went all around it. I know that when we went to do the check of the Nis Corps I went there for four days with the general, up to Bor, because once he assumed his duty he had to go and visit and inspect the Nis Corps. It took us four days to do that. I went back to Pristina. He remained in Nis for a while, and then he came back to Pristina too. So it's very difficult for me to say it, where he was on any given day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My impression of the evidence, and this will require detailed review in due course, but my impression of the evidence is that General Pavkovic spent more time in Kosovo during the war than in Nis. Is that a fair reflection of your understanding of the position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in general terms I would be more inclined to say that it was equal because the area of Kosovo, if you look at the area where the units were, this area was smaller, but there were more units there, and the tasks were more complex. So I would say that it was divided equally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The point I'm really interested in is whether when he spent so much time in Kosovo or at the forward command post that he might not be in a position to receive the reports when they were submitted from the Pristina Corps to the 3rd Army in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was at the forward command post of the 3rd Army in Gracanica. As for the reports that General Stojimirovic had in Nis, that he received there, those were the ones that we received at the forward command post of the 3rd Army, and the General was aware of that. So when he stayed in Nis, he had access to the reports of the Pristina Corps in Nis, and when he was in Pristina he either had direct contacts with the commander, or through the forward command post of the 3rd Army he had it in Gracanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not entirely understanding this arrangement. The -- let's go back to what you said about the normal reporting system. Did I rightly understand that reporting was from the Pristina Corps to the 3rd Army command, or have I misunderstood that? That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what was the arrangement to relay Pristina Corps reports to the forward command post of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to give an answer now as to whether the report went through Nis and whether we got it again, General Stojimirovic's report, or whether it went directly. It is hard for me to say now. I'm not sure. I'm not sure about that. But what is for sure was that we had the report that was sent to the General Staff from the 3rd Army. That is to say that at the forward command post, we had the information that had left the 3rd Army and was sent to the General Staff. That we knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were, in April 1999, put -- nominated as chairman of a commission to investigate allegations about inappropriate and arbitrary behaviour in Istok. Could you look please at P1721. This is -- this is your report of the 14th of April, the commission having been set up on the 13th of April, and this report is signed by you. Who were the other members of the commission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were about seven or eight members of this commission. The ones I remember are General Stojanovic from MUP, from the Ministry of the Interior, a general. Then -- then I think there was Lieutenant Colonel Pesic. I didn't even know these people, but I remember in respect of the document. And we were in contact with Vlahovic, Boro Vlahovic, the chief of SUP in Pec. I think that's what his name was. We were in contact with him. As for the members of the army, there was Colonel Stojanovic, the chief of security. Colonel Pesic was supposed to go, but he didn't for some reasons. Probably he had a previous engagement. And that was the team that was there as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this your personal report or the report of the commission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in a way, this is a report that mostly General Stojanovic and I agreed upon as to how this report would be worded, but I signed it as head of the commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that General Stojanovic of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Of the MUP, yes. I think his name is General Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: From what you've said, there were two members of your commission by the name of Stojanovic, one from the MUP and one from the VJ. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It has been suggested to us that normally a report of a commission like this would be signed by all the members of the commission. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in a way it is. It could be considered that way if this were to be done officially on the basis of a commission depending on what it is that you want to achieve. However, since we had established in terms of the basic task, why I went down there and why the commission went, there were no camps in the territory of Istok. I practically after that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, and we can deal with the factual position separately. I'm just trying to establish the propriety of the way in which this was carried out, and it might be better if I ask you a different question. How many of the commission specifically saw this and agreed with its terms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all of those who were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who were they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: That means General Stojanovic, Pesic, Stojanovic from -- from the military, and I. Practically the four of us. As for the Pesic from the army, I've already said that he didn't go at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had a considerable volume of evidence about the anti-terrorist operation in the summer into the autumn of 1998, and we've had reference to a plan and stages of a plan, and I think we've had evidence that there were three stages to a plan, and then we've had evidence that there were five stages to a plan. Can you explain or clarify this for us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a plan -- well, this original plan, this initial plan that was done in accordance with the order of the army commander, at first it had three stages. At first it had three stages, and then -- and then it was expanded by another two stages, so it was five stages altogether. As far as I can remember, the first stage was smashing the Siptar terrorist forces in the border area that in July was around -- it wasn't around. It was five kilometres. And it was the army that was the mainstay. The second stage was smashing the Siptar terrorist forces along the road of Pec, Decani, Djakovica, Prizren -- or, rather, at the border behind the border belt where the mainstay was the MUP, and the army was there to provide support. The third stage was smashing the Siptar terrorist forces along the roads, the three roads leading from Kosovo to Metohija. The mainstay was the MUP and support was provided by the army. It was those three initial stages. The fourth stage, as far as I can remember, was breaking up the terrorist forces at their main strong holds, namely Drenica. Now it is off the roads, so it's Drenica, Baranski Lug, Malisevo, Bajgora, Jezerce, Kosmac, and that is where operations took place later in several stages yet again because the terrorist practically came back to the same places, and practically operations were repeated two or three times in the same locations, so that would be the fourth stage. As for the fifth stage, that is the period when I was given the task by General Pavkovic in relation to the arrival of the OSCE mission when we kept the border. The army was responsible for the border and for in-depth security of the border with seven or nine combat groups. I'm not sure now. I think it was nine. I think it was nine. Nine combat groups and three company-level units at the critical points, namely Kramovik, Dulje, and Iglarevo. Those were the three companies that the army kept. We didn't -- well, at Batlava, later on a unit from the 15th army brigade was later sent to Lake Batlava. That would be it. And I know that the MUP had about 30 points throughout the territory at that time because we in the command drew that on the plan, and we marked our own deployment and the deployment of the MUP forces in order to ensure further coordination. That would be it, this plan in five stages that is referred to, that we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said which organ, whether it was army or MUP, was responsible for each stage except the fourth stage. Was it the MUP or the army that was mainly responsible for breaking up the terrorist forces at their main strong holds, namely Drenica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: According to the decision, when General Pavkovic came back from Belgrade on the 30th of May, when he went to Belgrade for the first time, I remember that, and the second time was what I already mentioned, the 21st of July. Now, in the meantime whether he went, I don't know, but I remember him going on those two occasions, that's for sure. I know that after the decision made by the supreme council, he said to me that the MUP would be the mainstay of the combat operations and that the army -- I remember this. This is exactly what he said to me, that the army would support in an adequate way. I remember that word. I remember him using that word. So for the most part this had to do with the support of the MUP except for the border area.
