In the border belt, I said that it was the army that was the mainstay and that the army in accordance with the decision of the Chief of General Staff and the army commander, was deploying reconnaissance, police, and other units there and preventing arms and ammunition from being brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 47, line 15. I believe the witness said that the army would support in an adequate way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is on the tape. That is what the interpreter said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does the word or the name "Grom" have any relevance in connection with these stages of this plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Because this part, the first three stages fully fit into the decision of the Chief of General Staff in terms of Grom '98. I know that full well because I worked on these documents together with the command organs. So this completely fits in these three stages. Later on, the second stage that is referred to in Grom, it was not carried out practically in 1998. That is mobilisation. There should have been mobilisation, but that was not carried out. In 1998. I'm talking about 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who devised the plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Which plan do you mean? The first one, this one, or Grom '98?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought you indicated that Grom '98 was the first three stages of this plan. Have I misunderstood that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Three plus -- yes, you understood it right. Plus -- plus mobilisation, the mobilisation that had been envisaged in case there was a deterioration in the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who devised the plan which ultimately had five stages?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: That plan -- well, the command of the Pristina Corps got a task from the army command when -- when General Pavkovic and General Samardzic went to Belgrade. So that plan -- well, it was ordered up there for the army to device this plan; I mean, for the army to work out the basic postulates of that plan, and then command to the Pristina Corps when the general came back, and he gave me a task that we start preparations for preparing the idea-based solution of that plan. Once this conceptual solution was worked out, then it was verified at the army command, at the General Staff, and on the basis of that plan, later on Grom '98 was devised in part. I'm saying that for the following reason: I'm know that around the 15th of July, the 15th of July, this plan was submitted to the General Staff, as well, the General Staff. As far as I heard, General Smiljanic in the 1st department -- the 1st administration. The general told me a copy had been made for the General Staff, and it was there for their use, and on the basis of that Grom '98 followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know if the Supreme Defence Council decided on the policy that this plan implemented?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. I think the answer is yes. When General Pavkovic returned from the meeting, that's what I heard from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know anything of the circumstances in which Mr. Sainovic was given certain responsibilities in relation to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know that Mr. Sainovic, on the 30th of May, I did not have information to the effect that he attended the meeting in Belgrade because when the general returned on the 30th of May, I asked him who attended the meeting. I was interested, quite simply, to see who attended, and he said, everybody, and I said, who is everybody, and he said, as for our guys, General Perisic, General Dimitrijevic, Samardzic, and I. As for the MUP, he says, the minister was there. Then he said Rodzo was there, Obrad, and Luka. That's how he addressed General Lukic and Obrad Stojanovic. And -- and as far as I can remember, he said to me that Stanisic was also there. Now, Sainovic and Minic, I don't think he mentioned them then. I don't think he did. It was only the second time when on the 21st, when he returned and when we talked on the 22nd, then he mentioned that Sainovic attended the meeting on the 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not clear about certain elements of that answer. When you said to me that you thought that the Supreme Defence Council decided on the policy and that's what General Pavkovic said when he returned from the meeting, is that a meeting that took place on the 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't know who he got information from, but he told me that the supreme council made a decision on adequate engagement. I assume that it was with the army commander, who else, that he talked to about this. It's probably from the army commander that he received this information and that he got it from the chief of General Staff. I don't know how he got this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You then referred to the 30th of May. What --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was your reason for referring to the 30th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the first meeting. I know when the general came back from Belgrade with General Samardzic and the chief of General Staff, when they went to see President Milosevic, first they went to the army command, and he took the planned -- plan for the deblockade of roads, and then that plan was taken to Belgrade to the chief of General Staff, and then certain corrections were made there, and then with this plan for the deblockade of roads, they went to see President Milosevic. That is how I understood him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that -- that this may have been the beginnings of what became the Joint Command, the coordination or exchange-of-information body?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in a way, I've said that on the 13th of May we had already informed the army command that there was no good cooperation and coordination with the MUP, especially at the border where the army was receiving tasks, and they did not have good coordination because the terrorists were getting in through the border without us being linked up with the MUP. We asked for this problem to be resolved, for someone to give an order to authorise someone. And then General Samardzic, as I've already said, authorised General Simic and General Pavkovic as the protagonists of cooperation and coordination in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, this passage of evidence began with me asking you what you knew about the circumstances which led to Mr. Sainovic having certain responsibilities for Kosovo. Do you know what led to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of authority was given to Mr. Sainovic. I can just talk about what I had heard, what he discussed. What kind of authority he was given I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've been given a document which bears to record answers that you gave in an interview with the Office of the Prosecution here. I don't at the moment intend to explore the circumstances of that with you, but just to ask you one thing about it. In -- in that document, you talk about a decision by the Supreme Defence Council to send Sainovic and the others down to Kosovo. Now, what did you mean by saying that to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I said to the OTP at all. As a matter of fact, I think that the investigator didn't even ask me about that. The investigator never asked me that. I'll tell you what the investigator asked me, but it wasn't this. How could I know at that time whether the supreme council had appointed him or President Milosevic? I could not know that, and how could I know that? First of all, it is certain that I never said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Without looking at what authority Mr. Sainovic actually had, who did you understand gave him authority to exercise certain functions in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is not something that I know or that I could know, but I can tell you what issues he dealt with. That I can tell you. But as to who gave him this authority, I don't know. I can share with you my impression that I got on the basis of this exchange of information at those meetings. I did get an impression, but first of all, I had not been introduced to Mr. Sainovic at all, but I knew from the media that he was the deputy prime minister, that that was the function that he had. When he went down there, I simply provided his political function. I did not give him or accord to him any kind of command function because nobody told us at the meeting on the 22nd that somebody was the commander, that this was the command, or anything. The -- immediately, the exchange of information started. And this was the context in which I viewed Mr. Sainovic, as the man who was in charge of the foreign policy aspect, and this is the only way in which I see him to this day. Eight or nine years later, I don't know. And I'm sure that in 1998 he did not issue any orders, verbal or written, either to the corps -- or, rather, I'm talking to the corps because that's what I know, or to me personally or to General Pavkovic to do anything apart from what was ordered by the 3rd Army commander. This is what I can say, and I can give you some facts to corroborate that. When General Lukic called for helicopters to evacuate a pregnant woman and an injured police officer from Kijevo, he talked to General Pavkovic asking him for the military to provide the helicopter. So that was in July, as early as in July. When General Pavkovic said that he had to consult the army commander to see whether this could be done, the army commander did not approve it, and when the briefing was done, when the exchange of information was done, that's what Mr. Pavkovic said, and Mr. Sainovic didn't say anything. They don't make any comments, and then General Lukic said, fine, Pavkovic, we'll deal with that, and they sent their own helicopter to evacuate the injured police officer and the pregnant woman from Kijevo. I recall this event quite clearly, and that led me to form an impression. It's not that I thought that the army should not provide the helicopter for the evacuation of those people from Kijevo because I personally was sure that the helicopter should have been provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've lost track of that account, I think. You said that Mr. Sainovic did not say anything, and then General -- and I think you gave the name, said fine, we'll deal with that. Who did you refer to, which general?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now look, please, at P2086. Look at the next page so that you have an idea of what it is. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it bears to be a document produced by the Joint Command. Was this something which emerged from the meetings of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. It is partially connected to it because at one point there is a mention of it, but it was mentioned quite some time before that in communication between the army command and the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you could look, please, at the paragraph number -- or the section numbered 2. You will see that that deals with the role of the Ministry of the Interior and then the role of the army, and then 2a, if you can see part of 2a -- oh, you haven't seen it yet. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's turn to the B/C/S page, please. You'll see reference there to the MUP and then to the army, and if you go -- if we go on to the next page, please, in both languages, and there you'll see that section 2a deals with civilian protection. And if you go to section 3, you'll see there the reference is to Municipal Staff. It's very much a document dealing with the roles of a number of organs. What was the role of the Joint Command in devising this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, leafing through my notes, I found at one place that Mr. Minic repeats something that General Pavkovic said about an order by the army commander to organise the defence of the inhabited areas through a document dating from either late June or early July 1998, and then he repeats what General Pavkovic said about this order for the mobilisation and the defence of the inhabited areas. So this is the context in which Mr. Minic mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with drafting the document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not personally, but I do have an opinion. To this day, I don't know how this document was done, how it was drafted, but this is a document that certainly was not done at that time, in 1998, in June or July, that's for sure. This is a document that could have been with some of the operations officers. This looks to me like a -- like a training exercise for how to do the defence of inhabited areas. I first read it when I came to The Hague from the beginning to the end, and to my mind this instruction was only amended in such a way that just Kosovo and Metohija is mentioned. Everything else can refer to Kosovo and Metohija, anyplace there or anywhere in the state. So this is not a specific instruction. It's like an instruction on how to operate a weapon. This is not a combat document, and it is not binding on anyone. It does not oblige anyone to perform any of the tasks that stem from this document. For instance, if I were the recipient of this instruction, it would assist me because I would then recall some elements that I may have forgotten to do if I was in charge of defending an inhabited area. So that would be the extent of the assistance that I would get from this document, and I would not be obliged to do anything that is listed herein or to accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that not make it very strange that the cover of the document is now headed "Joint Command for Kosovo"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that we probably did have an instruction of this kind, but the operations organ of the Pristina Corps did it. I think we had it from one of our organs. I probably wasn't able to know all of it because I was there for a year, but other organs, the administration of the Ministry of Defence, for instance, probably had it because they needed it more than we did at the Pristina Corps command. So that is my understanding, that this instruction came from the defence ministry administration for Kosovo. They may have made some amendments to perhaps invoke some kind of a fictitious authority for those duties and obligations to be taken more seriously because the problem of defending inhabited areas and towns was a major problem. And the state security organs were reporting to the -- to General Lukic, General Pavkovic, and everybody else who attended those meetings. They were reporting this to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you look now, please, at P1269. Now, you see that this is -- has handwriting on it. Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting. I couldn't really be certain. I am aware of the document, and I think that I actually -- if you allow me to look at the initials, I may have drafted this or written this document when I read it through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you did draft it. Your initials are on it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's very much on the face of it a document appearing to command both the VJ and the MUP and, indeed, talks about the Pristina Corps commander resubordinating MUP units. What was going on in this order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember when it was that I did it, when the general mentioned those detachments, because he told me -- he gave me some guidelines as to how I should draft this document, and he told me to mention those detachments and those MUP units. And then I said, well, we can't order them. You see that they don't accept our orders. And he said, just write it down; I spoke to General Lukic; just write this down. And this is what I did. I wrote this down, and it was sent to General Lukic for his information, this document, personally for him, for his information, because there are some tasks and some obligations that the army and the MUP were supposed to carry out together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give us a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll just complete this stage before we take a break. This -- this document on the screen has the numbers of specific MUP units or detachments in it. What was the source of that information, Mr. Djakovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean for the figures, who was the source?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I received that from the MUP organs. So I personally -- when actions were coordinated, they would tell me specifically which detachment was supposed to be used. So this was mostly done by General Obrad Stevanovic. He mostly designated or decided which PJP unit would be where. I think that at the time he had the authority to do so by -- from General Lukic. I don't know what their powers were, but I would be told by him for the most part which detachment would go there when we made the coordination and when we drafted various documents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A couple of problems with the transcript. Page 6, line 12, the date should be 1998. Page 15, line 8, that has actually been corrected. And page 29, line 21, the first word of the question should be "who." I can only apologise for exceeding my time limit, but that concludes the examination that the Trial Chamber proposed to conduct at this stage. Do you have questions, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do any Defence counsel have questions? At least one nodding head. If you wish to go out with the areas explored by the Trial Chamber, then you should indicate the areas that you wish to explore so that we can judge whether it's right in all the circumstances bearing in mind who's calling this witness to allow you to do that. However, you should feel free to cross-examine on any issue that has been raised in the course of that examination. Mr. Djakovic, we need another break at this stage. That will be for half an hour. We'll resume at 1.00. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher while we have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I begin my questions I had a question for the Court. Two matters. One relates to Exhibit P1468, which you're well aware we have a number of translation entries where it's indicated that the original is illegible to the translator. Now, obviously this man is the author of this document probably could furnish us a lot of help, but there are dozens if not scores of those. Sometimes it's only one word, and in the context it may not mean much, but sometimes it's a whole sentence or a whole section is, and because I don't know what it is, I don't know whether it's important or how important it is. Now, I don't makes sense for us to take up all our time at 10.000 euros an hour or whatever it would be, but I wonder if there might be some kind of procedure where the Court might direct this witness at the conclusion of his evidence as assistance to the Court just to sit down with a language assistant or maybe somebody from the Registry or the court staff and just read those portions so they could be written down, and then we would have an accurate record of what was written in his notebook. I propose that for your consideration. It's obviously not something you need to decide today, but I put it out there. The second thing, Your Honour, is Exhibit P2943 is the unsigned statement that Phil Coo and two others from the OTP wrote up when they interviewed General Djakovic in 2004. I may ask him a few questions based on that document. I have a B/C/S copy, and I would propose to give it to him at the end of the day so he can take it and read if he wants to because I anticipate I'm going to take more than 45 minutes and go into tomorrow. So I bring it up now rather than trying to scramble at the end and bring it up as he's leaving the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't seen anything or heard anything about time constraints with regard to this matter. I don't know if we're operating under normal time constraints or what. It might be helpful to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Hannis has indicated informally that he's going to use an hour and a half. He's certainly going into tomorrow as you've heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that partly depends, Your Honour, on what you decide about my proposal regarding P1468 because if you don't then I may want to spend part of my time trying to identify the most interesting or intriguing illegibles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. We could perhaps return to that tomorrow when we've had a chance to think. I'm looking, for example, at the moment at Rule 71 and wondering whether it might provide a device for doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- that's a procedure that might apply and might ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If it's only a question of the witness amplifying as best he can and only confirming where he can read the document and that's fully recorded, it would not on the face of it give rise to any unfairness unless passages were identified which might say something specific against the case of an accused who might want to cross-examine not the terms used but the -- the merits of the actual comment itself. So it's -- it would need to be done before the witness left The Hague. And the other alternative is for you to identify the ones that really matter and to deal with them in the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah. And as I said, to some extent I can look at some and say, well, that one doesn't matter because it's one word in the context of what appears to be otherwise clear, but as I indicated there some entries where there's an entire sentence missing or a bullet-point entry, and that could be extremely important or not important at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll hear parties on this first thing tomorrow morning once we see where you're going and once everyone's had a chance to think about the issue. Mr. Ackerman, it's difficult until you -- you embark on your cross-examination to determine whether the time is being used in the overall context reasonably. We're very reluctant to impose a restraint in advance on this. What Mr. Hannis is proposing in broad terms seems acceptable, and in light of that you might feel that your own case merits a similar allocation of time. It would be difficult to argue with that. But I can't give any more precise indication until I see just how relevant and direct the questions are. You'll bear in mind that the Chamber's questions were almost exclusively open questions of a brief nature, and the tendentious elements of this witness's evidence may yet be to come. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. You --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the post you held in 1998 and 1999 and told us that you retired 31 December 2001. Could you tell me what post you held between the end of the war in 1999 and your retirement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Between the end of the war and my retirement, I was deputy head of administration upon completing the national defence school. That happened for three or four months, and then I was appointed chief of the security administration of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia. After that, I became deputy head -- or, rather, deputy commander of the 1st Army, as I stated previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Early on this morning, you told Judge Bonomy that the handwriting in the notes of the Joint Command meeting after the 21st of October were done by Colonel Tesevic, and you told us at page 7 -- or page 8, line 6, today that you talked to Colonel Tesevic and you assigned a task to him in relation to archiving the documents and gave him an order, put that notebook in the archives. Were you the one who actually tasked him to attend the meetings and keep notes after October 21st?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He's my deputy, too, in the department, and it is on that basis that he attended the coordination meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you never gave that notebook to Colonel -- or General Stevanovic -- Stefanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't recall telling that to Phil Coo, an investigator from the OTP who interviewed you in 2004?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand you. What was it that I said to Philip Coo?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He indicates in what's Exhibit P2943, at paragraph 36, that you said you gave the notebook to Colonel Radojko Stefanovic, and he then put Colonel Tesevic in charge of the notebook. Does that refresh your memory or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: You are right. That is to say that at that time I expressed my doubt. I wasn't sure whether that's the way it was because afterwards when talking to Colonel Tesevic and Colonel Stefanovic, who came only in December to this position, rather, he replaced me only in December, so around the 20th of December he took over from me up until the 20th of January. There were a lot of holidays in that period of time, so it went on for almost a month. Then I had a break until the 20th of February, and then I went to Nis to take over from General Mladenovic, which is to say that it is correct that I had stated that, but I also stated that I cannot remember with certainty. He called me a second time, but I didn't have this information even then because I did not have documents to that effect convincing me either that I was right or wrong. However, General Stevanovic definitely could not have had the notebook in his hands because it was placed in the archives on the 24th, and the documents were sent to the army on the 2nd of November, 1998, and sergeant -- sergeant -- well, the sergeant in charge of the office handed it over. This was at the army command. And the other one handed it over to Belgrade after the new year. That was the route taken, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Bonomy asked you early on a couple of questions about the accuracy of your note-taking and whether you were taking a full account. After the meetings, did you ever review your notes with General Pavkovic to be sure that you had gotten the important points down correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. No. The general never asked me to do that, and he never used that notebook except when I was preparing for him an outline to inform General Samardzic about security matters. I prepared similar points for Colonel Djindjic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the first name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and then he transferred this to the army commander because the army commander personally expressed his interest in terms of what this was all about, in the field of security that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about during the meetings or after the meetings? Did you ever ask any one of the speakers to clarify something you might have written down, for example, Mr. Minic or Mr. Sainovic or General Lukic? Did you ever --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I jotted down what I managed to jot down the way I understood it, and basically it was for my personal use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- and when you weren't clear, you sometimes put a question mark by an entry if you weren't sure you'd heard correctly, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that did happen, but only if it had a certain effect on something that I thought would be a problem for me within my functional duties, and perhaps sometimes I would discuss that with General Pavkovic because I only contacted him about such matters. And sometimes when the army commander would call me for approving plans, then I would discuss that with him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The point I'm trying to make is I -- from my impression of you during your testimony this morning, it seemed to me you're an intelligent, articulate guy who takes his work seriously. So were you comfortable that the notes you were taking were generally accurate and reflective of what was said at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what? I tried to jot down what I could. However, some things I simply omitted, what I thought that I did not need. I can say that straight away, that I was least interested in the foreign policy factor, if I can put it that way, because as the assistant for operations and training, I didn't need that part at all. I was not involved in politics at all, so I recorded very little of that when speaking of that factor. When speaking of security as a subject matter, when the people from state security were providing information, I didn't even write down a lot of what General Pavkovic said because for the most part I knew that, or I knew what General Lukic said. I was more interested, for instance, when Mr. Minic said certain things in relation to the functioning of the municipal authorities, the municipal staffs, then the districts. Then often I was interested when Mr. Andjelkovic spoke about civilian protection and things like that because after all, this did have something in common with my own functional duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Related to your duties, you mentioned at page 15, line 18, today that -- what you called the operational report, and you said the first one you drafted was on the 10th of July, and this -- and this --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- as I understand it, had to do in connection with your dealings with -- with state security and trying to get information from them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to show you an exhibit. It's P2945. This is a -- this is newspaper article, an interview with General Stojanovic -- or Colonel Stojanovic, and I want to go to page 2 of the B/C/S. I think it's page 10 of the English. In that newspaper article, he talks a little bit about the Joint Command, and you'll see on that page the item number 2 that's inserted. I don't know if we can blow that up so you can get a better look at it. We need item number 2. Yeah. You can make it a little bit bigger, perhaps. It's dated the 11th of November, 1998, at the top. I will tell you it's from the Pristina Corps Command Security Sector, and it's a report to the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Did you ever see this kind of report from Colonel Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can barely see this. It is unintelligible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he prepare -- did he personally prepare reports that went to the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. No. All his reports went through me. No one could go apart from the operative organ because the operative organ is the realiser of coordination with organs outside the military, and the commander is responsible for coordination according to the rules of the land forces. Since I'm subordinated to the chief of staff, as for this function of coordination, I carried that out within the command. Stojanovic could go attend meetings with the MUP and the state security, but only with regard to professional expert matters that had to do with the use of equipment and methods of security organs. Since I was head of the department, I knew that he had the authority to do that, and I knew that he could freely contact the organs of state security and the MUP organs with regard to specific security-related problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you a similar or a related kind of document. It's Exhibit P1197. This is another sort of report about security matters to the Joint Command or from the Joint Command in late 1998. I'll ask you to take a minute when it's on the screen and tell us -- I guess we need to go to the second page of the B/C/S. In my English translation, this is Joint Command, 20 November 1998, and it's described as an Operations Report. Just looking at that first page, can you tell us, did you ever see reports like this in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: These are reports that we wrote in the command of the Pristina Corps. That is to say that on the basis of discussions that I referred to previously, I asked General Pavkovic to try to look into the matter with General Lukic and state security and see whether we could get their information so that we within the command could carry through the requests of the army commander and the corps commander, and the general said that he would first discuss this with General Lukic and Gajic, and then from the 10th of July he -- he provided that information in handwriting. He obtained it. And I was fair because I gave them the documents that pertained to the military, to them, so that they could follow the overall situation in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is this the kind of report, then, that you wrote on the 10th of July, an operations report like this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's it. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I see the number at the top, "Strictly confidential number 1142-134." Is that number 1142 something that was related to the Pristina Corps in late 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: It's our number. It's our number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I understand the numbering system with the VJ documents, then that number 134 is the 134th document in this series related to operations reports for 1998, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly, but it is also possible that some document of a similar nature may crop up. It doesn't have to be a daily report. This in essence is a daily report, but sometimes during the course of one day there would be two reports that would be similar. So I do not rule out that possibility, say, that 110 and 111 would appear for the same date. That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now -- but in general these were -- generally speaking, these were daily reports, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. These were summarised reports of the Ministry of the Interior and of the state security as they provided them in the first part. That is to say, they were copied verbatim. We didn't change a word. And in the second part, it would be the report of the military. And these reports put together that way joined up were sent to the mainstays, and one copy would remain in the Pristina Corps for the sake of analyses that we carried out afterwards. So this was proper working material for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, by my rough math, if you wrote your first one on the 10th of July, 1998, and there was a single report for every day, by November 20th you would be on or at number 134, right? Because there's approximately that many days between the 10th of July and the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly, but I do not rule out the possibility that on some days there were no reports and that we didn't receive any because we wrote reports on those days when we would receive reports from the MUP and the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, who did you receive the information from in the MUP that went into these reports?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned the names of the persons with whom I cooperated from the MUP. Now, who did this within the MUP I don't know, but from Gajic about state security and most often it was Adamovic from the MUP. Now, who it was that did it there, it was probably an entire team. And I have to say that this is not a combat document. It's not even an operative document. This is only operative by way of content. It contains operative information. However, not according to any rule, and for years I was engaged in this kind of operative work. This kind of document is not prescribed. It is also not prohibited in terms of communication between certain entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To whom was this report distributed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: So this report was always sent to the three mainstays, the MUP, the DB, and the army. And while I was there until the 14th of October, it -- these reports were not to send to anyone apart from the three mainstays. And when Colonel Tesevic replaced me at that post, when he managed the data, he -- that was our arrangement, if anyone were absent for a longer period of days so as to miss a number of meetings, that this should be sent to those people in the political structures. And as he informed me later, he sent this to Mr. Minic. The reason he quoted was because he had been absent from Kosovo for a period of maybe 10 to 15 days, and he missed maybe four or five meetings, and he sent this to him by way of a reminder of some of the activities that were being carried out at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did other members or attendees of the Joint Command meetings receive copies of these? Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Andjelkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, because they were for the most part present. They were aware of these problems, and there was no need for anyone who was present there to get this kind of a report or information because they had already been told about all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. You mention that to your recollection I think the first time you used the term "Joint Command" in a document was on the 6th of July, 1998, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you seen the original of that document since 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I couldn't have seen it. I saw a copy in the course of my preparations, and I was actually trying to trace back the origins of this name. I know how to go about it, so I tried to see how far it dated, and I did have some assumptions. So the first date was the 13th of May where cooperation and coordination with MUP is mentioned, and then the next one is the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Joint Command was mentioned at the 13th of May meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, not at that time, but in our assessment document, it is sought that the cooperation and coordination with MUP should improve, and then what followed was the order from the army commander authorising General Pavkovic to coordinate some actions, activities with other entities. MUP is not actually named as such. The term that was used was "entities" in the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before we go to that further discussion on the July 6th document, one last question about this operation report on the screen. Who -- who decided to title this "Joint Command"? Whose idea was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: In this case it was my idea. On the basis of the conversation, let's say, of the document dated the 6th of July, then the one that's dated the 10th of July followed, I decided to put "Joint Command" analogous to the previous document on those -- for this coordination activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we next look at Exhibit P2113. I don't know if you might have seen this one before or not, General. It's from the 125th Motorised Brigade. It's dated the 7th of July, 1998, and you'll see the commander of this brigade is issuing an order to subordinate units where he says in item 1: "I prohibit the execution of any operations by units and formations without the approval of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija and my own approval." You will see in the first paragraph above that, he says "Pursuant to the order of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija strictly confidential No. 1104-6 of 6 July 1998 ..." That document 1104-6 is I think the one that you've been telling us about, the first one that you wrote using the term "Joint Command." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know where that -- where the original of that document might be?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: In the archive. It has to be in the archive. The document has to be in the archive. All the documents that are logged in must be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you told us in your testimony earlier that document had to do with what -- how VJ units were to be used, or what was it about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That pertains to the prohibition of the use of the army and MUP units without the knowledge of the Joint Command, but I explained to you what I meant when I used the term "Joint Command." I meant General Lukic and General Pavkovic, no one else, because no one else in the chain of command could issue orders to the MUP units apart from General Lukic and to the army units apart from General Pavkovic or General Samardzic. So as far as I was concerned, there was no one else that was meant by this term that I use here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But prior to sending out this order from the 6th of July, was there any advance notification or explanation to subordinate units about what the Joint Command was or who the Joint Command was, or did you just send out that order on the 6th of July entitled "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some people contacted me knowing that I mostly did the documents, the command organs that were subordinate to me, so some of them contacted me. I wouldn't even rule out the possibility that the commander of the 125th and of the 549th actually called me and asked me what is this in reference of, and I explained to them that this was an authorisation for them to coordinate some actions with the MUP. Without this order on the coordination, they could not carry out any combat actions in such a way, and that is why in this order it is explicitly ordered. You can see here where there is the reference to the previous order. It says: "Without the MUP staff and the command of the Pristina Corps." So the two are separate, the MUP staff and the corps command. So I wrote that advisedly so that they should know that there were two levels of command involved in this coordination, the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps Command. And I think that Zivanovic contacted me, and I told him that if he doesn't receive a document where it says "Joint Command" and that coordination had been carried out, he could not move any of his units regardless of who asked him to do so. And they knew that. They respected that. Even the army commander issued a similar order previously from the level of the army command about the prohibition of the use of units without his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel Zivanovic, or General now, Zivanovic was here and testified at page 20508 and told us generally that when he received this order he called you because he didn't know what this was about or what the Joint Command was, and, General, he -- he told us that you explained that the Joint Command for Kosovo referred to coordination at the highest level and that in the future he, Zivanovic, would receive similar unsigned orders from the Joint Command. Was that right? Is that consistent with your memory of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part. I know that I and General Zivanovic, well, we are good friends, and I know that he would not have said something like that had it not happened, but I mostly explained to all of the people who were asking themselves what it was, those who received similar documents, and I was telling them that in essence this was in lieu of the coordination plan that we were supposed to do, that the coordination was carried out in this manner, which was simpler and was much better tailored to the MUP and to the army. That was the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did that document, number 1104-6, of 6 July also go to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. There was no need. No, no. The one from the 125th. You mean 1104-6. No, no, there was no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't mean the one from Zivanovic but the one that he had received from you, which I understand is --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I know. I know. No, there was no -- definitely it didn't go there because I personally drafted it and I know that it didn't. Because every time it went out, I put my initials and the addressees on all my documents. In 99 per cent of the cases, you can find the initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Since it didn't go to the MUP, I'm having a hard time understanding why it said "Joint Command." Why didn't it just go out from the Pristina Corps Command if it's going to Pristina Corps subordinate units? It seems like you're just creating needless confusion by introducing this new term "Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, excellent, yeah. No. No. Colonel Zivanovic, when he showed the document with the words "Joint Command," the MUP received the same document from General Lukic. And then when they realised that both commands agreed about the duties of the two segments, then they start implementing those activities. Without that, any member of any MUP detachment or anything else couldn't accept any duties if he didn't know that General Lukic and General Pavkovic had not agreed on the coordination, not the two of them personally but their assistants in appropriate departments. That was the essence of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If I understand correctly, then you're saying there was a similar kind of document that went from General Lukic out to subordinate MUP units about not taking any action without approval of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I personally don't know if General Lukic did that, but I assume that he should have regulated in some way how his organs would learn that this was -- that this had been coordinated by his assistants. As I said, that was General Stevanovic, Redja [phoen] Mijatovic, Adamovic, they coordinated this with us so that they could know that this had been coordinated and that they would receive support from the army because the essence is in this: The army commander would not allow the army units to move if this had not been coordinated fully regarding the support to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we will have to interrupt you at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I clarify with Defence counsel which counsel definitely will cross-examine? Mr. Aleksic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that my cross-examination will not take long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have any questions, I won't have more than three to four, but I don't think I will have any questions, unless Mr. Hannis springs any surprises on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can see that I have just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we definitely have cross for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Djakovic, we have to interrupt our hearing at this stage because another case is heard in this courtroom this afternoon, and we cannot, regrettably, continue. We will however, resume tomorrow at 9.00 in -- back in this courtroom at 9.00 tomorrow when your evidence will continue. It may well be completed tomorrow. I can't tell you for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I hand him a copy of the B/C/S version of P2943 if he wants to look at it? I might ask some questions from it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind me what that is, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's the B/C/S translation of his unsigned statement to Phil Coo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes. You're being given a translation of the statement that it is said the Prosecution took from you, and we would be assisted by you spending at least some time between now and tomorrow morning reading that to familiarise yourself with its terms. Between now and tomorrow morning, it is vital that you have no communication with anybody about the evidence in this case. You can talk to people about whatever else you like, but you must not discuss the evidence in this case, any aspect of it. Could you now please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will see you tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
